---
title: "Quiz: graphs, cuts and maximum flow"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A graph has nodes $s, a, b, t$. How many s–t cuts does it have? List them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$s$ is always in $S$ and $t$ always in $T$. Each other node can go either way.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2^2 = 4$: $S = \{s\}$, $\{s, a\}$, $\{s, b\}$, $\{s, a, b\}$ (and $T$ is the rest).
:::

---

**Q2.** The edge $b \to a$ has capacity 7. In the cut $S = \{s, a\}$, $T = \{b, t\}$, does it count?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which direction does it cross?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. It goes from $T$ ($b$) to $S$ ($a$). Only edges from $S$ to $T$ count in the cost of the cut.
:::

---

**Q3.** Someone claims a flow of value 12 in a graph that has a cut of cost 10. Why must they be wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
All flow from $s$ to $t$ has to pass the cut.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every unit of flow from $s$ to $t$ crosses the cut from $S$ to $T$, through edges whose capacities add up to 10. Flow coming back from $T$ to $S$ only lowers the net amount. So every flow has value at most 10.
:::

---

**Q4.** The flow on $u \to v$ is 3, its capacity 5. Which arcs does the residual graph have between $u$ and $v$, and with which capacities?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One arc for room left, one for flow that can be undone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A forward arc $u \to v$ with residual capacity $5 - 3 = 2$, and a backward arc $v \to u$ with residual capacity 3. Pushing along the backward arc reduces the flow on $u \to v$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Ford–Fulkerson stops when there is no path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph. How do you read off a minimum cut?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which nodes can you still reach?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$S$ = the nodes reachable from $s$ in the final residual graph, $T$ = the rest. Every edge from $S$ to $T$ is full, and every edge from $T$ to $S$ carries no flow, so the cut cost equals the flow value: both are optimal.
:::

---

**Q6.** All capacities are integers. Why does Ford–Fulkerson stop, and why is the final flow on every edge an integer?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the bottleneck of a path if all residual capacities are integers?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If all flows are integers, all residual capacities are integers, so every bottleneck is a positive integer, at least 1, and the new flows are integers again. Each step raises the flow by at least 1 and the flow cannot exceed the (finite) capacity of any cut, so the algorithm stops after at most that many steps.
:::

---

**Q7.** A graph has two different minimum cuts. You raise the capacity of one edge of the first cut. Does the maximum flow increase?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Max-flow = min-cut. What is the minimum cut after the change?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The second cut still has the same cost, and the flow can be no larger than it. To raise the maximum flow, every minimum cut must get more capacity.
:::

---

**Q8.** An image has $10^6$ pixels and each pixel is a node. Why is enumerating all cuts out of the question, and roughly how large is the graph that max-flow has to handle?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count cuts, then count edges per node.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
There are $2^{10^6}$ cuts. The graph, however, has only $10^6 + 2$ nodes and a few edges per node (4 neighbours, plus one edge to $s$ and one to $t$), so a few million edges. Max-flow algorithms work on that directly, in time polynomial in the size of the graph; on image graphs this typically takes about a second or less.
:::
